messages.author: d0591fb2a98d1e44
messages.subject: Bad Convergence and help improving my model
parts:
Hi all,

I'm having a bit of trouble with my model. It's not a simple model as the goal is to multiple three matrices together and then by a row and column vector. To give two values one between 0 and 1 and one close to 0. The estimates are reasonably good, off by .01 to .02, and I'd like to improve that, as MLE gets to .001 or .0001. I've uploaded my code and outputForDebugging2.txt has the results from my last run. The convergence could be better and the n_eff value is relatively small despite the number of iterations, chains, etc. How can I improve my model's convergence?

Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bad Convergence and help improving my model
parts:
The Bayesian posterior mean only approaches the posterior mode
in the limit of increasing data.

Did you verify that Stan's MLE gives you what you expect?

I don't understand the goal of the model --- why are those
matrices constrained to lie in (-1.05, 1.05)? This can
be very problematic computationally if a lot of the probability
mass is near the boundary.

For efficiency, you probably want to make all those transformed
parameters local variables. And you want to vectorize as many
of the distributions as you can and reduce the loops to matrix
operations wherever possible.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bad Convergence and help improving my model
parts:
> On Mar 11, 2016, at 1:29 PM, Daniel Berman <daniel....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I have been using Matlab's MLE and that gives me what I expect with pretty good accuracy. However, Stan's estimates are slightly worse than Matlab's.

Which estimate from Stan are you talking about? The optimization
result? Those should be the same, at least up to several digits,
assuming you've coded the model properly.

>
> The 1.05 was something I set recently. Previously I had constrained it to be between -1 and 1, but I was worried that it would be problematical computationally if the actual value was near 1. However, physical constraints require that the values be between -1 and 1.

Then you absolutely need to constrain it to be between -1 and 1 if
that's required. Otherwise, Stan's HMC will devolve into a random
walk for values near -1 or 1. Either way, if there is a lot of mass
near -1 or 1, the sampling can be difficult if you're talking about HMC.

>
> I had trouble making all those transformed parameters local variables because the final result of the model, Gmeasured and GmeasuredImag are the results of much of the transformations. As a result, I was very unsure of how to do that. If you have any advice, that would be very helpful.

Functions and/or locally scoped blocks. If you do this

real final_result;
{
real temp;
.... compute ...
final_result <- ...
}

then temp is a local variable and not included in the results.
> Again, vectoring was something that I was having trouble getting to work and was something that I intended to get eventually.

It can make up to an order of magnitude difference in speed
(or more in multivariate cases) due to shared computations
across the items.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bad Convergence and help improving my model
parts:
Stan also supports MLE calculations, by the way. It's
just called "optimizing" as it finds the posterior mode
(which is the MLE if the prior is uniform).

The problems near boundaries are just due to numerical
stability of the transforms. For instance, we log constrain
positive values, but this only gives us an effective
range of (-320, +320) or so in the unconstrained space,
beyond which we overflow or underflow. So we either have
to take small steps, or deal with a lot of rejection because
Stan's HMC is only using the gradient (first-order derivatives)
with multiple steps to simulate the Hamiltonian, which has more
curvature (higher-order derivatives).

We need to get all this written up in a user-facing way.

- Bob

>
> We need to get all this written up in a user-facing way.
>
> Is it possible that changing to a probit scale (changing [-1,1]->[0,1]->[-inf,inf]) would help at all?

Very unlikely. But we do have the Phi_approx inverse unit-normal CDF
you could try if you think it might help.

> Which estimate from Stan are you talking about? The optimization
> result? Those should be the same, at least up to several digits,
> assuming you've coded the model properly.
>
> The estimates from Stan I'm talking about are the ones using the priors I set. Matlab's MLE results are better than Stan's Bayesian results and I'm not sure where I'm going wrong.

I'm not sure what you mean by "better" here. The MLE isn't
going to match the posterior mean in many models, and in some
cases they can be very different. What you want to check is that
your posterior intervals are calibrated (50% of the 50% intervals
contain the true parameter values under simulation).

- Bob
